# Playbook

**Hiding.** Don't default to the middle cell every round — 5 is the most predictable guess on a 1–9 line and I paid for it repeatedly. When I'm the target, randomize across the full range, avoiding both the center and edges. If my opponent's shots show a pattern (e.g., always firing the same cell), exploit it; when they have no pattern, vary my own position so I can't be profiled.

**Firing.** Don't fire the same cell round after round at the same target just because it hit once. A single early hit locked me into cell 5 forever, and every later shot at that spot missed. When I fire at a target repeatedly, cycle cells — favor cells near where they've hidden before only if their hiding shows clustering; otherwise spread shots out. Each shot at a new cell carries fresh information; repeating a known-miss cell wastes it.

**Claims.** Always claim the true result. Bluffing a hit risks exposure through cross-checking and buys nothing (the payoff comes from the shot landing, not the claim). This worked and I keep it.

**Harbor.** Never fire on Harbor. The 3-point jettison payout is outweighed by the removal threat for the rest of the patrol. Ignore Harbor as a target entirely.

**Escort/salvage.** This is where I left points on the table — I claimed "none" every round and scored zero from the 5-point mutual escort pool. Next time: coordinate explicitly through my station note. In round 1, post a proposal like "Echo proposes mutual escort with Gamma this round" and then, if the other boat's note doesn't reject it, name them at the salvage stage. Even a one-sided attempt costs nothing; a successful pairing is worth more than a hit (5 vs 4 points). Keep renewing the pairing each round in the notes.

**Notes.** Use them as a coordination channel, not a placeholder. "Steady on station" every round was wasted bandwidth — it should carry my escort proposals and any observed shot patterns worth sharing or misleading about.

**Standing orders.** Follow the firing order (it's validated anyway), but remember the real score comes from hits (4), escort pairs (5 each), and avoiding being hit (−1). Escort coordination is the highest-value untapped lever — prioritize it from round 1.

1.text:
PLAYBOOK

- Escort claims are the biggest reliable payout: 5 points per boat per round, more than a hit. When the escort stage is put to me, I always name a boat, never none. I try to coordinate implicitly with the boat that isn't firing at me (or use my station note to signal a partner, e.g. "holding with Echo"), and I keep naming that same partner every round so a mutual pattern can lock in. I left this entire revenue stream on the table by always claiming none.

- When the hide stage is put to me, I never repeat a cell I've already used, and I don't default to the middle of the range (5). Middle cells are where a lazy shooter fires. I rotate through off-center cells like 2, 4, 7, 8, weighting toward cells my hunter is unlikely to pick. If a hunter has hit me at a cell, I never go back adjacent to it next round.

- When the fire stage is put to me, I don't fire the same cell every round even if it worked once — the target adapts. I spread shots across the target's plausible cells, and I track which cells my target has hidden in before (from past hit/miss results) to avoid re-firing cells that already missed.

- When the claim stage is put to me, I always report the true result. There's no gain to lying (the office knows the truth and the claim must match), so truthful claiming costs nothing and keeps me clean.

- When the note stage is put to me, I use the note for something: either a steady neutral pattern that gives nothing away, or a deliberate signal toward the boat I want as an escort partner. Filler notes like "steady on station" were wasted signal bandwidth.

- Never fire at Harbor: the 3-point payroll comes with a permanent removal threat, which is strictly worse than the payoff.

- Follow the standing firing order for targets — it avoids retaliation cycles — but treat my own hiding cell, shot cell, and escort claim as the three places where I actually create value. Points came from hits and escort claims; the escort column is the one I systematically ignored and should never ignore again.

2.text:
**Playbook for the sonar picket game**

**Escort claims are the money.** Mutual escort claims pay 5 points each to both parties — more than a hit (4 points). Every round I claimed none and threw away 25+ points across six rounds. From now on: name another boat every single round, no exceptions. Prioritize the boat that is not shooting at me this round and that I am not shooting at (so Echo and Foxtrot pair off when I'm Gamma's target). If notes allow signaling, propose an escort pairing explicitly in my station note ("Gamma escorts Echo; Echo escorts Gamma?"), and read others' notes for the same. Never claim none — the downside is zero, since a one-sided claim appears to cost nothing.

**Hiding: stop playing the same cell.** I hid at 5 repeatedly and got hit by Foxtrot three rounds running. If I take hits in consecutive rounds, move far — switch corners or the opposite end of the line, not an adjacent cell. Avoid midline 5; everyone defaults there. Randomize between edge cells rather than settling into any fixed cell.

**Firing: stop firing at 5.** I fired cell 5 every round and only hit when the target happened to sit there. When my target's location is unknown, vary the fire cell each round and avoid the modal cell everyone else guesses. If a target hit me from a known pattern, consider firing at the cell they just hit me from (people often stay put after scoring).

**Claims: always report truthfully.** The claim is validated against the office's private result anyway — lying gains nothing and burns credibility. This part of my play was correct; keep it.

**Never fire on Harbor.** The payroll transfer of 3 points is tempting, but Harbor's threat of removal for the rest of the patrol kills all future earnings (hits plus escort payouts). Leave Harbor alone for the whole game.

**Standing order on targeting:** follow it unless there's a decisive reason not to — deviating from the announced rotation makes my shots predictable to whoever reads the log, and the log is public. The rotation itself tells everyone who's shooting at whom, which is exactly the information I need to pick escort partners.

**Points arithmetic, final check:** with six rounds of mutual escort claims (5/round) plus any honest hits (4 each), ~30+ points is achievable. My +6 came almost entirely from two lucky hits. The gap is the escort game — that's where I play next time.
